Exorcist
EK-sor-sist
noun
From the Greek exorkistēs, from exorkizō, “to adjure, to bind by an oath” — from ex (out) and horkos (an oath). The exorcist bound spirits by a solemn adjuration, a formula sworn over them.

Biblical Definition

An exorcist in the Authorized Version is one who adjures evil spirits — who tries to drive them out by a sworn formula, a set of powerful names pronounced over the possessed. The Greek root is an oath: to exorcise is to put under oath, to bind a spirit by adjuration. The one place the word appears in the KJV is a warning, not a warrant. “Certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13). Seven sons of Sceva tried it — the name of Jesus used as a technique, borrowed like a spell, spoken by men who did not belong to Him. The demon was not deceived: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?” (Act 19:15). Then the possessed man “leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded” (Act 19:16). Here is the whole doctrine in one bruising scene: power over the powers of darkness is not in a formula but in a Person, and He is not on loan. The name of Jesus is not a charm to be conjured with; it is the confession of those He owns. Paul cast out devils because Christ dwelt in him; Sceva’s sons only chanted, and were stripped and beaten for their presumption.

Webster 1828 Definition

One who claims to expel evil spirits by adjuration or formula; in Scripture, a counterfeit exposed at Ephesus.

EXORCIST, one who pretends to expel evil spirits by conjuration, prayers, and ceremonies; one who adjures.

From Greek exorkizō, to adjure or bind by oath, from horkos, an oath.

The exorcist bound a spirit by a sworn formula of names pronounced over it.

The vagabond-Jewish exorcists borrowed the name of Jesus as a technique (Act 19:13).

The seven sons of Sceva were overpowered and fled naked and wounded (Act 19:16).

Key Scripture

Act 19:13 — "Then certain of the vagabond Jews, exorcists, took upon them to call over them which had evil spirits the name of the Lord Jesus, saying, We adjure you by Jesus whom Paul preacheth."

Act 19:14 — "And there were seven sons of one Sceva, a Jew, and chief of the priests, which did so."

Act 19:15 — "And the evil spirit answered and said, Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?"

Act 19:16 — "And the man in whom the evil spirit was leaped on them, and overcame them, and prevailed against them, so that they fled out of that house naked and wounded."

Modern Corruption

The one biblical exorcist is a cautionary figure, not a model; his power was borrowed and it failed.

expand to see more

The modern imagination, fed on film and horror, pictures the exorcist as a heroic ritualist wielding holy water and Latin against a snarling demon. The Authorized Version’s single use of the word points the opposite way: to the vagabond sons of Sceva, who treated the name of Jesus as a formula they could work without knowing the One who bears it. The honest drift is toward sensationalism — the exorcist as spectacle — and it obscures the lesson. Scripture is not interested in technique; it is interested in whose you are. The demon answered the incantation with a question that unmasked the whole trade: “who are ye?” (Act 19:15).

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition beyond that drift into spectacle. The principle to recover is that authority over evil spirits is not a method but a Master. Sceva’s sons had the right name and the wrong standing; they adjured “by Jesus whom Paul preacheth” (Act 19:13) as men quoting another’s password, and the powers of hell were not fooled. Christ’s own cast out devils by His indwelling Spirit and His finished work, not by an approved rite; and even they were told to rejoice less that the spirits were subject to them than that their names were written in heaven. The believer does not conjure with the name of Jesus; he belongs to Him, and that belonging — not any borrowed formula — is the whole of his safety. The story ends with the exorcists fleeing naked and wounded (Act 19:16), and with the name of the Lord Jesus magnified, and many burning their books of curious arts. Power is in the Person, never in the technique.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The word means one who adjures evil spirits by a sworn formula — and at Ephesus it names a failed counterfeit.

expand to see more

Exorcist — from Greek exorkizō, “to adjure, to bind by oath.”

To exorcise is to put a spirit under oath by a formula of names.

The KJV’s only exorcists are the vagabond Jews who borrowed Christ’s name (Act 19:13).

The demon knew Jesus and Paul, but not the pretenders — “who are ye?” (Act 19:15).

Power over evil spirits lies in the Person of Christ, not in a technique (Act 19:16).

Usage

"The KJV’s exorcist is no hero but Sceva’s son, chanting a name that was not his to wield."

"They adjured the spirit by Jesus whom Paul preacheth, and the spirit asked, “who are ye?”"

"The exorcists fled naked and wounded: the name of Jesus is a confession, not a charm."
